title: Chapter III

teacherSummary.text: Nick receives a formal invitation to one of Gatsby's parties, where hundreds of uninvited guests drink, dance and gossip about the host. With Jordan he meets the owl-eyed man in the library, amazed that the books are real. Nick talks with a young man who turns out to be Gatsby, with his reassuring smile and 'old sport.' Gatsby speaks privately with Jordan. Leaving, guests see a car wreck in the ditch. Nick describes his own ordinary life and his friendship with Jordan, who lies and is a careless driver.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter III,” how does Fitzgerald show Gatsby's party? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter III, how does Fitzgerald develop the idea of Gatsby's party? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter III develops the idea of Gatsby's party. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of Gatsby's party. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter III suggests about Gatsby's party. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's imagery and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how F. Scott Fitzgerald uses imagery in Chapter III to complicate the reader's understanding of Gatsby's party. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter III within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of Gatsby's party responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of Gatsby's party follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter III and its treatment of Gatsby's party. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's imagery and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter III as evidence for a larger claim about Gatsby's party in The Great Gatsby. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter III as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of Gatsby's party. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Great Gatsby.

Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Chapter III develops the idea of Gatsby's party. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Gatsby's parties are a performance that attracts people without making real connections. When the text says “In his blue gardens men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars” (Chapter III, paragraph 1), it shows this directly. Guests come "like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars," yet most never meet their host, and Nick, who calls himself "one of the few honest people that I have ever known," invites us to judge them.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
